newsitem.title: USA: Intel says it didn't steal Digital patents.
newsitem.headline: Intel says it didn't steal Digital patents.

text.p: Intel Corp said Wednesday it does not believe its Pentium computer chips infringe on Digital Equipment Corp's patents and reiterated that Intel will "vigorously" defend itself.
"DEC has stated that technology is vital to its business," Intel said in a statement. "Technology is vital to Intel's business as well."

On Monday, Digital Equipment sued Intel, alleging that the chipmaker infringed on DEC patents covering key chip technologies. Digital is seeking unspecified damages and will ask the court to halt Intel from shipping Pentium chips.
Intel spokesman Howard High said company executives would not comment on the lawsuit beyond the short press release issued Wednesday.
Intel shares continued to slump amid concerns that the lawsuit could cost the world's biggest chipmaker billions of dollars, analysts said.
In late afternoon trading, Intel shares were down 1/8 at 152-1/4. On Tuesday, Intel shares plunged 6-3/4 to 152-3/8.

To the surprise of some legal experts, Intel, so far, has not sued Digital back. Intellectual property litigators said countersuits are part of the usual defense against patent infringement complaints.

"It is inconceivable to me that Intel would not sue them back," said Michael Barclay, an intellectual property litigator at Wilson Sonsini Goodrich & Rosati, a Silicon Valley law firm that has been involved in several high-profile technology lawsuits.
Intel's High said the company only has had 24 hours to review the case and is "leaving options open."

Digital Equipment, based in Maynard, Mass., is claiming Intel based its Pentium chips -- the devices that serve as the brains of more than 80 percent of the world's PCs -- on 10 patents that were awarded to Digital between 1988 and 1996.
Digital sells the competing Alpha microprocessors, chips that work faster than Intel's offerings but which have had little success in the market against Intel's marketing might.
Digital claims that Intel's patent infringement caused it "economic injury and, if not stopped, would cause irreparable harm."
In huge advertisements in the New York Times and Wall Street Journal Wednesday, Digital said it filed the lawsuit "because technology is so vital to our business."
"We don't mind competing against anyone's technology -- except our own," the ads read.
Digital and Intel have said they will fight vigorously to prevail in court. Chances are low, however, that the lawsuit will ever reach the courts, several legal experts said.

"A lot of patent infringement suits do settle simply because of the costs of the lawsuits," said Margreth Barrett, intellectual property professor at Hastings College of Law in San Francisco. "The suits go into very technical matters" and it takes a lot of time and money to educate the judge and jurors.
